FIXED 2026-08-23 (PR #306, bdbd8b6). ELEVEN PAGED READS ACCEPTED AN UNBOUNDED CALLER-SUPPLIED PAGE SIZE; TWO ALREADY CAPPED IT, SO THE CORRECT PATTERN EXISTED IN THIS CODEBASE AND WAS SIMPLY NOT APPLIED.

⚠⚠ CORRECTION TO THIS ROW'S OWN COUNT, and it is the reason LL-015 exists. The original title said TWELVE while its own enumeration listed ELEVEN - the two never agreed. The set was re-derived before the fix by TWO independent sweeps: every `.Take(` call site under src (20 total), and every request type declaring a caller-supplied page/limit (13 files). Both agree on ELEVEN, and NEITHER WAS COMPLETE ALONE - the first is what catches the audit endpoint, which pages with a local named `size`; the second is what confirms no record-declared paged read was missed. The eleven: GetActionsRegister, GetAdrsRegister, GetBacklog, GetDependenciesRegister, GetDocumentsRegister, GetInvariantsRegister, GetMissionsRegister, GetRisksRegister, GetTemplatesRegister, the audit list endpoint, and GetDecisions.

THE SHAPE. Each guarded only the LOWER bound - `pageSize = request.PageSize <= 0 ? 25 : request.PageSize` - then called `.Take(pageSize)`. Nothing rejected or clamped a large value, so an authenticated caller could request an arbitrary page size and the query would attempt to materialize it.

HOW IT WAS FIXED. ONE shared guard, `PageSize.Clamp`, beside `PagedResult` in Acmp.Shared - not eleven copies of a per-query constant. DEF-059's rule applied again: an invariant asserted at one entry point and absent at the others is the shape this codebase keeps paying for, and one helper means the twelfth read cannot forget. Verified on origin/main: 11 clamp call sites, ZERO lower-bound-only guards remaining.

WHY Max = 500, recorded because it is the one judgement call. It is the largest page the application itself ever requests - the kanban's KANBAN_PAGE_SIZE, the reports and dashboard ALL, and the wiki list - and ADR-0022 records that pageSize=500 was VERIFIED to cover every register at this deployment's size (CON-001 caps the committee at 20 users). So the cap bounds an unbounded materialization without narrowing anything the product legitimately does. A cap of 50, copied from GetNotifications, would have broken reports and the kanban: a behaviour change dressed as a fix.

ONE DELIBERATE NON-CHANGE. GetDecisions with a NULL limit still performs no Take. That read is not caller-amplifiable - with no limit it reads the register once, which is what the reports page needs - so introducing a cap where none existed would have been a silent truncation, DEF-103's own shape, rather than a fix. Only the value the CALLER supplies is bounded there.

THE GUARDS, and they share no mechanism (LL-009). PagedReadCapTests discovers paged request types by REFLECTION and requires each to be acknowledged - a hard-coded list of what exists would have to be updated by whoever forgot to clamp, which is the failure mode itself. PageSizeTests proves the MECHANISM by driving a real handler with int.MaxValue. Both mutation-proven with COMPILING mutants: reverting one register to the old guard kills the behavioural test; dropping one name from the acknowledged set kills the reflection test - one test each.

⚠⚠ THE REFLECTION PREDICATE WAS WRONG ON FIRST WRITE AND ITS OWN DISCOVERY GUARD CAUGHT IT. Keyed on the OUTPUT shape - request types returning PagedResult<T> - it structurally EXCLUDED GetNotificationsQuery, the one read that was already correct, because that one returns a bespoke DTO. A discovery that cannot see a correctly-shaped read cannot see a future BROKEN one shaped the same way, so the narrowing was the whole failure. Re-keyed on the INPUT shape (any request carrying an int PageSize). This is LL-015 firing inside the very fix that LL-015 was born from.

FIXED 2026-08-23. INV-013 NAMED 'branch protection' AS ITS ENFORCEMENT MECHANISM AND NO BRANCH PROTECTION EXISTED ON main - NOT CLASSIC PROTECTION, NOT A RULESET, NOTHING. Measured by three independent endpoints rather than one, because inferring from a single endpoint is the proxy failure LL-006 records: /branches/main/protection returned 404 'Branch not protected', /rulesets returned an empty array, and /rules/branches/main - which reports the rules ACTUALLY applying to a branch from every mechanism - also returned empty. Nothing required a pull request, a review, or a green check before a commit reached main, while the package asserted the opposite as fact in five places, one of them an INVARIANT: INV-013's enforcement column ('branch protection; CI; git workflow'), SEC-120, SEC-126 ('cannot merge/deploy without passing' - flatly false), SEC-172 and SEC-581. An invariant whose named enforcement does not exist is enforced by discipline alone while the register describes that discipline as machinery - DEF-010's manufactured-assurance shape, and the family of DEF-078's healthcheck that evaluated zero checks.

HOW IT WAS FOUND, and the observable is the transferable part: not by auditing the invariant but by trying to execute DW-078. Across twelve open pull requests NOT ONE reported mergeStateStatus BEHIND, and BEHIND is the status GitHub reports only when a repository requires branches to be up to date. THE THING THAT GAVE IT AWAY WAS A STATUS THAT NEVER APPEARED, which is far harder to notice than a wrong value, because absence produces no output to be suspicious of.

THE FIX, applied on the operator's decision in the same interview: classic branch protection on main with required status checks backend, frontend, compose, e2e, secrets, sast, trivy-fs, trivy-image and sbom; strict=true so branches must be up to date, which is what closes the stale-green hole this row was found through; enforce_admins=false so the operator retains the direct-push path their 2026-08-20 branching decision depends on for package, prompt and memory writes; required_linear_history=true; force pushes and deletions off.

TWO CHOICES INSIDE THAT CONFIG THAT WERE READ OUT OF THE SYSTEM RATHER THAN GUESSED. FIRST, 'publish' IS DELIBERATELY NOT REQUIRED: it reports SKIPPED on pull requests, and a required check that never reports leaves a PR pending forever - a gate that cannot be satisfied is as broken as one that cannot fail. SECOND, THE PATH-FILTER HAZARD IS NAMED HERE SO IT IS NOT REDISCOVERED AS A MYSTERY: ci.yml's pull_request trigger ignores only *.md, but e2e.yml's and security.yml's also ignore tamheed-package/** and .claude/**, so a pull request touching ONLY package paths would skip seven of the nine required checks and hang. That is acceptable because package writes go straight to main by the operator's rule and never form a PR, and because admin bypass resolves it if one ever does - but a future session finding a package PR stuck should read this sentence rather than start debugging CI.

THE FIX IS PROVEN, NOT ASSERTED: immediately after the change all twelve open pull requests moved from CLEAN or UNSTABLE to BEHIND. The control went from never emitting that status to emitting it on every pull request, which is the same discipline as LL-013's fault injection - the number moved, so the instrument has a subject. It also establishes retroactively that all twelve were behind the whole time and six of them were reporting CLEAN.

RESIDUAL, CARRIED AS DW-081 AND NOT SILENTLY CLOSED: SEC-120 states 'Minimum 1 approver (lead or peer)' and required_approving_review_count is set to 0, because GitHub forbids self-approval and this is a one-human team, which makes that clause unsatisfiable rather than merely unmet. Configuring 1 would have blocked every merge including this project's own. The clause needs either a second reviewer or a corrected sentence, and that is the operator's call.

FIXED. THE APP TYPECHECK HAD BEEN COMPILING BY ACCIDENT SINCE BEFORE THIS BRANCH, AND THE vitest 3 to 4 BUMP REMOVED THE ACCIDENT. `tsconfig.app.json` sets `types: ["vite/client"]` and includes all of `src`, and FOUR test files under `src` legitimately read the repo from disk - LoginPage.test.tsx, styles/contrast.test.ts and the two rtl-*.test.ts guards import `node:fs`/`node:path` and use `__dirname`. Node types were never declared for that project. They arrived TRANSITIVELY: vitest 3 re-exported types from `vite`, whose dist/node/index.d.ts carries a `/// <reference types="node" />`, and that registered @types/node globally for the whole program. vitest 4 restructured its types and the chain is gone, so `tsc -b` produced 16 errors over code nobody had touched - TS2591 `Cannot find name 'node:fs'` and TS2304 `Cannot find name '__dirname'`.

FIX: declare it. `types: ["vite/client", "node"]`, with the history written into the file, because an accidental type dependency is one dependency bump away from a broken build and restoring the accident would only defer this. VERIFIED on the branch's OWN install after a clean `npm ci`: `npm run build` exits 0 with zero errors, and the full suite is 158 files / 1309 tests passing.

MY FIRST DIAGNOSIS WAS WRONG AND IS WITHDRAWN. This row originally read: the local build reports 16 errors while CI compiles the same commit cleanly, therefore the local environment is at fault and trap 22b's named arbiter is unusable on this machine. Every clause was wrong. THE EXPERIMENT THAT PRODUCED IT WAS INVALID: I checked out `main`, ran `npm run build`, saw the same 16 errors, and concluded main was broken too - but node_modules still held the BRANCH's install, so I was compiling main's source against the branch's dependency tree and calling it a test of main. A checkout changes the source; it does not change node_modules.

WHAT ACTUALLY ADJUDICATED IT, and it is the transferable part: the e2e job failed with the SAME SIXTEEN ERRORS, in Linux, in CI, inside the web image's `npm run build`. That killed the local-environment theory outright. The three-way split then located it exactly - main source with main's tree passes (231 packages), branch source with the BRANCH's tree fails (169), and branch source with MAIN's tree PASSES. Identical source, different tree, opposite verdicts: the variable was never the machine.

WHY CI'S `frontend` JOB LOOKED GREEN ON THE BRANCH AND WAS NOT EVIDENCE: it fails at the coverage-gate step, which runs BEFORE the build step, so `npm run build` never executed there at all. A job that stops early cannot vouch for the steps it never reached, and reading its failure as 'the build is fine, only coverage is red' would have been a second wrong inference from the same run.

APPROVING AND PINNING A LESSON DOES NOT MAKE IT BIND - THE BINDING NOTE IS ONLY REBUILT BY `handoff_emit`, AND NOTHING COMPARES THE TWO. LL-016 was Approved, pinned and attributed to the operator on 2026-08-23 and was STILL ABSENT from tamheed-package/CLAUDE.md on 2026-08-25, two days and several sessions later. That file is the note every session loads at startup and is the ONLY mechanism by which an approved lesson reaches a future agent, so for those two days the register said LL-016 binds every session and the sessions never saw it.

HOW IT WAS FOUND, by accident rather than by any check: `handoff_emit` was run to publish five newly approved lessons, and its diff added SIX lines - the five plus LL-016. Before the run the note carried LL-001 through LL-015 with LL-016 missing; nothing anywhere had flagged that.

THE SHAPE IS ONE THIS PROJECT HAS ALREADY RECORDED IN ANOTHER PLACE: a row's lifecycle_status and the artifact that is supposed to reflect it are UNRELATED, and no gate, readiness rule or view compares them. DEC-064 d2 said 'DW-037 is ACTIVATED' while the row itself still read Open, and the same class of gap is here between `lessons.lifecycle_status = Approved, pinned = 1` and the rendered note. `lessons-confirmed` cannot see it either - that advisory counts PROPOSED rows, so it goes green the moment a lesson is approved, whether or not the approval ever reaches anything that binds.

SEVERITY, stated honestly: medium. No product behaviour is affected and no gate is wrong; what fails is the propagation of a control the operator has explicitly paid attention to. The cost is silent and delayed - a lesson approved to prevent a repeat does not prevent it, and nobody learns that until the mistake recurs.

REMEDIATION APPLIED NOW: the note is rebuilt and carries LL-016 through LL-021. THE STANDING FIX IS PROTOCOL, NOT CODE: run `handoff_emit(target_dir=<repo root>)` in the SAME batch as any lesson approval, and commit the resulting tamheed-package/CLAUDE.md with it. A mechanical version - a readiness rule comparing the pinned set against the note's rendered ids - would be the durable answer and is not attempted here, because the note is tool-owned and the rule would belong to the plugin rather than to this package.

CARRIED **OPEN AT HIGH SEVERITY BY OPERATOR DECISION** (`DEC-077` d1) - READINESS IS DELIBERATELY **FALSE** UNTIL THIS IS CHASED. The backend job died twice in the Testcontainers SQL Server path on commits that changed no backend code, and a plain re-run of the same tree then passed. `main` is green again at 6acbb89. What is NOT settled - and what keeps this row open - is whether the cause is environmental or a real intermittent in the only test that exercises FREETEXT against real SQL Server.

(2) 6bdaac4: FAILURE - `Acmp.Integration.Tests.SearchProvidersFtsTests.Every_provider_executes_its_full_text_query_on_real_sql_server`, the SQL Server container dying at startup with '** ERROR: [AppLoader] Failed to load LSA: 0xc0070102 ... `Acmp.Api.Tests` RAN 6x SLOW AND FAILED 17 OF 368 ON A COMMIT THAT TOUCHED ONLY FRONTEND TEST CODE - EVERY FAILURE A 100-SECOND `HttpClient` TIMEOUT, SCATTERED ACROSS TWELVE UNRELATED TEST CLASSES. THE MEASUREMENT, NOW THREE RUNS DEEP AND SANDWICHED. `Acmp.Api.Tests` on this branch: `4a79c33` **3m18s, 368/368**; `34f9a83` **20m35s, 351/368**; `cb2c946` **2m37s, 368/368**. Baseline on `main` is 3m6s and 3m17s at 368/368. **The failure is a single 6-8x outlier between two normal runs.** Every failure in it is `TaskCanceledException : The request was canceled due to the configured HttpClient.Timeout of 100 seconds elapsing`, and the 17 are spread over TWELVE classes - Votes, TopicEndpointsCoverage, Topic, Minutes, Audit, UserManagement, Traceability, Session, Risks, Research, GuestWindow, Decisions - with no shared feature, endpoint or fixture. A defect in the code under test does not distribute itself evenly across twelve unrelated areas; a starved runner does.

THE DELTA BETWEEN PASS AND FAIL CANNOT EXPLAIN IT. `34f9a83` changes ONE file, `src/Acmp.Web/.../columnPrefs.test.tsx` - frontend test code, a different job on a different runner. It cannot reach `Acmp.Api.Tests`. The backend tree was byte-identical across a 3m18s pass and a 20m35s failure.

⚠⚠ THE MITIGATION CANNOT BE CREDITED, AND SAYING SO IS THE POINT. `cb2c946` shortened the forcing tests' sleeps (600s -> 30s, 300s -> 60s) as a no-regret bound on any abandoned docker build, and that run was green. **But the run BEFORE the mitigation was also green, with `RUN sleep 600` still present.** So the green run does not evidence the fix, and the register must not read it as one - two greens either side of a red say the environment, not the change. `LL-018`'s rule applies: a pair of observations that is weak evidence about WHERE a fault lives is not made strong by one of them being after a change.

`Acmp.Integration.Tests` WAS FINE THROUGHOUT, AND THAT MATTERS TWICE. It passed 62 of 64 in 1m58s in the FAILING run - faster than the passing run's 2m46s - which rules out general Docker degradation as the story, and means `SearchProvidersFtsTests` was GREEN, so `DEC-077` d3's stop rule did NOT fire on this red. It also means `DW-084`'s container guard and `DW-085`'s image-build guard both ran clean on a real runner.

WHAT WOULD MOVE THIS ROW. A second occurrence with the same signature - `Acmp.Api.Tests` far over its ~3-minute baseline with scattered `HttpClient` timeouts - appended here with run id and commit. Until then the honest state is one environmental outlier, recorded rather than re-run into silence.

FIXED (PR `#315` -> `2b0da29`). The kanban column count was localized for the eye and not for the ear; the criterion that excused it is superseded by `AC-148`.

WHAT WAS WRONG. `AC-147`'s fourth exclusion read *"a number reaching an ATTRIBUTE rather than a text node is outside what was swept"* - a true statement about what I did and an INVALID exclusion, because this project's definition of done says **a surface that DOES NOT EXIST can be excluded by name in a `Met` verdict; a surface that EXISTS but is unproven CANNOT.**

THE SWEEP I HAD DECLINED WAS SIX EXPRESSIONS. A raw number reaches a human-readable attribute only through a template literal or a concatenation, because anything routed through `t()` is localized centrally by the formatter module. Two greps over `aria-label|title|alt` cover the whole surface: FOUR template literals, one of which interpolated a quantity, and TWO concatenations, both via `t()`. **An exclusion is a claim about a surface's SIZE, and it is cheap to check before writing it rather than after.**

THE ONE INSTANCE. `Kanban.tsx` built a column's accessible name with `col.cards.length` interpolated RAW, twelve lines above the same number rendered through `<Num>`. So in Arabic a sighted reader saw the localized digits and a screen-reader user heard Latin ones - one number, one component, two answers. Fixed by routing it through `t()`, which is the ONLY path that reaches the central formatter; a template literal cannot. `Kanban.test.tsx` asserts the ACCESSIBLE NAME rather than the visible count, because only the accessible name could have caught it, and it is mutation-proven: restoring the template literal reddens that one test while the other twenty-one in the same file stay GREEN, since they all run in English where both forms render identically.

THREE NEIGHBOURS CHECKED AND DELIBERATELY LEFT ALONE, each correct for a DIFFERENT reason, which is why none of them was "fixed" alongside: progress bars carry the percentage as a CSS `inlineSize` and are `aria-hidden`, so nothing is announced; `role="progressbar"` sets `aria-valuenow`/`min`/`max`, which the ARIA specification requires to be PLAIN numbers that assistive technology formats itself, so localizing them would BE a defect; and an `<input type="number">` must hold a Latin-parseable value.

⚠⚠ A RESIDUAL THE OPERATOR MAY WANT TO RULE ON, recorded rather than hidden. `AC-148` supersedes `AC-147` IN SUBSTANCE - withdrawing an exclusion makes a criterion WIDER, hence a different criterion rather than a reworded one - and `AC-148` carries its own `Met` verdict (`AV-226`) against `2b0da29`. Sixteen older ACs in the register DO carry `superseded_by` with `retired_in`, so the column is used - it simply cannot be set through the tool today. **The supersession therefore exists in PROSE ONLY, and a column nothing sets is invisible to every view** - `DEC-064` d2's shape, where a decision said a row was activated while the row still read `Open`. The practical consequence is that `NFR-037` now has TWO active criteria, both `Met`, one of which contains a withdrawn exclusion a future reader could take at face value.

A TEST SHARED ONE OWNED VALUE-OBJECT INSTANCE ACROSS THREE NAVIGATIONS, AND ONLY THE .NET 10 UPGRADE REFUSED IT.

`DbBackstopTests.DecisionKey_Duplicate_IsRejectedBySql` handed the SAME `LocalizedString` instance to `Title`, `Statement` AND `Rationale`. Those are three SEPARATE owned entity types - `Decision.Title#LocalizedString` and siblings - so the change tracker was asked to track one CLR object under three identities. EF Core 8 tolerated it; EF Core 10 refuses: *"The property 'DecisionId' belongs to the type 'Decision.Statement#LocalizedString', but is being used with an instance of type 'Decision.Rationale#LocalizedString'"*, thrown from `NavigationFixer.SetForeignKeyProperties`.

⭐⭐ THE OLD GRAPH WAS NEVER LEGAL - THE RUNTIME UPGRADE ONLY STOPPED HIDING IT, which is `LL-017`'s ambiguity resolved in the *"the old one was lying"* direction. The test passed for a reason unrelated to its own assertion (that SQL rejects a duplicate `DECN` key), and it now actually reaches that assertion.

⚠ PRODUCTION IS UNAFFECTED, CHECKED RATHER THAN ASSUMED. `Decision.Draft` has exactly two callers - `RecordDecision` and `SupersedeDecision` - and both pass three DISTINCT request fields, which are separately deserialized objects.

⚠ THE SWEEP FOR OTHER INSTANCES IS THE SUITE, NOT A REGEX. 269 Domain + 1167 Application + 392 Api + the other 65 Integration tests all pass on `net10.0`, so this was the only site carrying the pattern. A grep for *"same variable passed twice"* is exactly the instrument that returns a true number about the wrong set (`LL-015`); the runtime enumerated it exhaustively instead.

FOUND BY: CI's backend job on `DW-080` phase A, PR `#320`. Fixed by giving each navigation its own instance. ⚠ The fix is NOT verified locally - the test needs real SQL Server via Testcontainers and the Docker daemon is down on this machine; build and `dotnet format` pass and CI is the instrument.

FIXED (PR `#320` -> `0939ccf3`, CI run 33125872560 backend job 98703773327 GREEN: 461 files, global line coverage 99.60%, zero files below 95%). THE TWO UNCREDITED LINES IN `WebexWebhookRegistrar.cs` WERE A GENUINELY UNEXECUTED PATH, NOT A COVERLET ATTRIBUTION ARTEFACT - AND THE FIRST FIX FOR IT WAS ITSELF RACY AND WAS REJECTED BY CI.

THE LINE NUMBERS, AND THE ARGUMENT THAT MADE A LOCAL REPORT USABLE WHILE DOCKER WAS DOWN. `Acmp.Application.Tests` was run ALONE in Release with CI's own `coverlet.runsettings`, after `rm -rf tests/*/TestResults` (`DEF-069`). It reported 25 coverable / 23 covered - CI's `92.00% (23/25)` EXACTLY. The argument is a SET argument needing ONE premise: the local tests are a SUBSET of CI's over the same build and collector, and coverage is monotone in tests executed, so the local covered set is a subset of CI's; equal counts then force the sets IDENTICAL. UNCOVERED: lines 30 and 31 - the `await EnsureAsync(...)` inside `ExecuteAsync` and its closing brace. Line 29, the `CreateScope()`, WAS credited.

⚠⚠ CORRECTION KEPT IN PLACE BECAUSE IT IS THE MORE INSTRUCTIVE HALF. An earlier version of this row, `PE-664`, and commit `1b79677f`'s message all justified that with *"`Acmp.Application.Tests` is the ONLY project whose tests reach this file"*. FALSE, AND NEVER MEASURED: `Acmp.Api.Tests` reaches it too and covers lines 42, 43, 44 and 63, because `AcmpWebApplicationFactory` boots the whole app. The conclusion was untouched - the subset argument never needed that premise, and `Acmp.Api.Tests`' covered set is itself a subset of `Acmp.Application.Tests`', so the union stays 23 and a SECOND project independently fails to credit lines 30-31. ⭐⭐ A VALID ARGUMENT RESTING ON A WEAK PREMISE IS WEAKENED, NOT STRENGTHENED, BY A STRONGER PREMISE YOU DID NOT CHECK. Filed as `LL-027`.

CAUSE OF THE ORIGINAL GAP - THREE STEPS, NO REASONING, AS THE ROW DEMANDED. (1) The HIT COUNTS answered before any experiment: `EnsureAsync`'s line 42 recorded exactly six hits, exactly its six direct unit tests, and line 44 exactly two, exactly the two disabled-path tests; the background-service test contributed zero. (2) Replacing that test's `DidNotReceiveWithAnyArgs` with a POSITIVE assertion failed - *"Actually received no matching calls"* - so the original assertion was passing vacuously. (3) `registrar.ExecuteTask` immediately after `StartAsync` read `status=WaitingForActivation` with a null exception: not faulted, never resumed.

FIRST-PARTY CONFIRMATION, WHICH IS WHAT SETTLED `LL-017`. Microsoft documents a .NET 10 breaking change, *BackgroundService runs all of ExecuteAsync as a Task*: before .NET 10 the portion of `ExecuteAsync` ahead of the first await ran on the MAIN thread during startup; .NET 10 dispatches the entire body to a background thread. That inline execution is what credited lines 29-31 under `net8.0`. So `LL-017` resolved toward *the old instrument was crediting something it should not have* - decided by a documented runtime change rather than by argument, on the very file whose history made the opposite answer look likely.

⚠⚠ THE FIRST FIX WAS WRONG AND CI CAUGHT IT - `StopAsync` IS NOT A SAFE JOIN. It passed locally at 25/25 and 1167/1167 and then failed on the runner with the same *"Actually received no matching calls"*. `BackgroundService.StopAsync` cancels the stopping token BEFORE awaiting the stored task, and under .NET 10 the body is dispatched carrying that same token, so on a loaded runner the work can be cancelled before the thread pool ever starts it and `StopAsync` then joins a task that did nothing. ⭐⭐ A FIX FOR A RACE THAT PASSES LOCALLY BECAUSE THE RACE WENT YOUR WAY IS THE DEFECT CLASS REPRODUCING ITSELF INSIDE ITS OWN REMEDY, and only CI could see it: the local machine wins that race every time.

THE LANDED FIX IS `ExecuteTask` ITSELF. It IS the running body; awaiting it involves no cancellation at all, so it is deterministic BY CONSTRUCTION rather than by timing, and it rethrows anything `ExecuteAsync` threw, which turns the test's never-throws claim from an assumption into an assertion. ⛔ Do not restore `StopAsync` here, and do not read a green local run as evidence for either shape - the runner is the only instrument that ever discriminated between them.

STILL FORBIDDEN, NOW FOR A STRONGER REASON THAN PRECEDENT: `[ExcludeFromCodeCoverage]` and lowering `ADR-0016`'s 95%. The test PASSED on both runtimes and the suite was green either way, because a NEGATIVE assertion is satisfied by the empty run; the per-file coverage floor is the only routine instrument here that measures EXECUTION rather than OUTCOME, so it alone discriminated. Both suppressions would have deleted the single working signal and left the empty test standing. Filed as `LL-026`.

SWEEP: `WebexWebhookRegistrar` is the ONLY `BackgroundService` in the repository and the only test of this shape - the one other `StartAsync` under `tests/` is Testcontainers' `container.StartAsync` in `ContainerStartup.cs`, unrelated.

NO PRODUCTION DEFECT. The registrar is best-effort by design (`ADR-0024`, and its own header): it never throws to its caller and retries on the next consent or restart. Ceasing to block host startup is the stated INTENT of the .NET 10 change.

⭐ MEASURED AFTERWARDS, WITH DOCKER UP, SO THE NEXT SESSION HAS A NUMBER INSTEAD OF A PROHIBITION: the FULL local backend pipeline run exactly as CI runs it reproduces CI's gate output exactly - 461 files, global 99.60%, gate exit 0. The local gate is a faithful model of CI's WHEN THE DAEMON IS UP; it is only unusable while `Acmp.Integration.Tests` cannot run. That one local run also surfaced `DEF-114`, unrelated to this defect.

FIXED. `DW-085`'s FORCED-BUILD GUARD REPORTED A FALSE RED ON ANY MACHINE THAT HAD BUILT IT BEFORE, BECAUSE DOCKER CACHES `RUN sleep 30` LIKE ANY OTHER LAYER. ⚠⚠ THIS ROW PREVIOUSLY NAMED THE WRONG MECHANISM AND SAID SO CONFIDENTLY - READ THE CORRECTION, IT IS THE MORE VALUABLE HALF.

THE REAL MECHANISM, ISOLATED BY A SINGLE-VARIABLE EXPERIMENT. Docker's build cache is keyed on the INSTRUCTION, not on the image tag. Once anything has built `FROM alpine:3.20` + `RUN sleep 30`, a rebuild of that same instruction returns in about TWO SECONDS under a BRAND-NEW tag - measured. The 10-second budget therefore never expires, `BuildOrFailFastAsync` returns normally, and the assertion that a hanging build must time out fails with *"no exception was thrown"*. CI never sees it because a fresh runner has a cold cache, so the guard rots only on a developer's machine - the worst direction for the one test that proves this timeout path at all.

THE FIX IS ONE LINE, AND IT IS THE INSTRUCTION AND NOT THE TAG: the generated Dockerfile is now `RUN echo {Guid} && sleep 30`, so the layer's cache key differs every run and the build must really execute. ⛔ A PER-RUN IMAGE TAG FIXES NOTHING - that was tried first and the test still failed, which is what exposed the wrong diagnosis.

⚠⚠⚠ THE CORRECTION, AND IT IS THE PART TO CARRY. This row first asserted *"Testcontainers does not rebuild an image that already EXISTS"* and stated that the layer-cache explanation had been *"measured and DISCARDED"* on the strength of a 33s identical rebuild against a 31s one-byte-different rebuild. **Both claims were wrong, and the second was the confident one.** Two faults produced it:
(a) A COLD-CACHE MEASUREMENT GENERALISED INTO A MECHANISM. The 33s figure was taken minutes after the Docker daemon started, with the cache cold. It was a true number about a state that no longer held (`LL-015`). Warm, the same build takes ~2s.
(b) A CONFOUNDED REPRODUCTION, WHICH IS THE STRUCTURAL LESSON. To confirm the image-exists theory I pre-created the named image and re-ran the test, and it failed identically in 804 ms. That felt like proof and it was the strongest-feeling evidence of the session. **But pre-creating the image did TWO things at once: it created the named image AND it warmed the `RUN sleep 30` layer.** The failure was caused by the half I was not looking at. A reproduction that changes two variables confirms whichever one you were already watching.

⭐⭐ WHAT ACTUALLY ADJUDICATED IT WAS THE FIX FAILING. The per-run-tag fix was applied against the true precondition and the test still failed - and that failure is the only reason the wrong mechanism did not ship. **An intervention that isolates one variable explains; a reproduction merely confirms.** Filed as `LL-029`.

HOW THE FIX IS PROVEN, AND WHY CI CANNOT ADJUDICATE THIS ONE. With BOTH halves of the failing precondition present - the orphaned `acmp/forced-build-timeout:test` image AND a warm layer cache - the class now passes 2/2 in 22s, where before it was 1/2 with *"no exception was thrown"*. That is a proper single-variable before/after: only the Dockerfile instruction changed. ⚠ **CI going green is necessary but NOT sufficient evidence here, because CI never had the failing precondition** - a fresh runner has a cold cache and this test passed there throughout. The local experiment is the proof; do not cite the CI run as though it validated the fix.

⚠ NOT `DEF-108` AND NOT `DEF-109`. Neither signature matches: this is deterministic, reproducible, and now explained.

THE /session SHELL RENDERS LATIN DIGITS BESIDE ARABIC-INDIC ONES ON THE SAME LINE - THE TWO Intl.DateTimeFormat CALLS NEVER GOT WBS-24.4'S NUMBERING PIN. In Arabic the agenda-slot card reads `10:40-10:55 · ١٥ دقيقة`: the TIMES come from Intl.DateTimeFormat built on the bare i18n.language tag and resolve to Latin digits, while the minute count comes through the i18n number formatter and resolves to Arabic-Indic. The expiry banner has the same split - `ينتهي 02/09/2026، 1:30 م` in Latin against file sizes rendered `٢٫٤ MB` two cards below. MEASURED, not inferred from the pixels: Intl.DateTimeFormat('ar') returns `07:40` and `01/09/2026` while Intl.DateTimeFormat('ar-u-nu-arab') returns the Arabic-Indic forms of both. THE FIX ALREADY EXISTS AND IS EXPORTED FOR THIS EXACT PURPOSE. numberFmt.tsx exports numberLocale(lang), whose own doc comment says it is exported because ANY Intl formatter that emits digits needs it, and it pins ar-u-nu-arab. The two /session formatters simply take i18n.language directly instead. WHY IT SURVIVED WBS-24.4, which is the part worth carrying: that item's census was of Intl.NumberFormat sites and of values handed to the translator, and its own scan script number-render-scan.mjs is recorded in its acceptance criterion as TRIAGE rather than a coverage proof - it had already been wrong three times, missing the reports family, then camelCase identifiers, then a number carrying a literal suffix. A DATE formatter emitting digits is a fourth shape it does not look for, and no unit test could see it either: jsdom does not render, and an assertion on formatted output agrees with whatever the formatter produced. ⚠ A SECOND CLAIM IS DISPROVED BY THE SAME EVIDENCE AND IS LEFT FOR WHOEVER READS numberFmt.tsx NEXT: that file's header states bare `ar` resolves to Latin digits under Node's ICU and Arabic-Indic IN A BROWSER, and offers that difference as the reason to pin. The screenshot that found this defect was taken in a real Chromium at 1200x900 and shows LATIN digits, so the browser half of that sentence is wrong - the pin is still right, but not for the stated reason. FOUND by the standing rule that a visual change must be LOOKED AT: every mechanical gate in the repository is blind to this. vitest, the per-file coverage floor, axe, check-i18n and the e2e sweep all passed over it, because nothing reads pixels and nothing compares one digit system against another.

title: THE COMMITTED SLICE-REVIEW SLATE GENERATOR REFUSES ANY WORK ITEM WHOSE TITLE NAMES OTHER THAN EXACTLY ONE ACCEPTANCE CRITERION, AND TWO ITEMS IN THE VERY SLICE IT WAS BUILT FOR NAME TWO AND THREE. scripts/gen-slice-review-slate.mjs derives an item's criterion by regex over the WBS row's own title and then calls fatal() unless the match count is exactly 1. Measured across SL-033: WBS-24.1, 24.2, 24.3, 24.6 and 24.7 name one criterion each and pass; WBS-24.4 names AC-147 and AC-148; WBS-24.5 names AC-149, AC-150 and AC-151. Both would abort the generator today. WBS-24.8 names NONE, because its title is the original specification text preserved byte-identically and the completion amendment that every earlier item received was never applied to it - so the generator aborts with 'names 0 acceptance criteria; expected exactly one'. WHY THIS MATTERS MORE THAN AN ERGONOMIC COMPLAINT: the generator IS the mechanism by which LL-011 is discharged. That lesson is pinned and the operator once REFUSED an interview for being given identifiers instead of records, and its remedy is explicitly that a generator prints every cited record from the canonical store. So an item the generator cannot render is an item whose review must either be hand-built - the exact thing LL-011 forbids - or not held. The failure is loud rather than silent, which is the one good thing about it, and it fails CLOSED. title: DEF-116 IS MARKED Fixed WHILE ONE OF THE TWO ROWS ITS OWN TEXT NAMES IS STILL UNRENDERABLE - THE FIX TRADED A COUNT GUARD FOR A SAMENESS GUARD AND NOBODY RAN IT AGAINST THE HARDER OF THE TWO CASES. But the widened code also added a guard asserting every criterion answers to the SAME requirement - 'one header cannot describe both' - because the section renders a single requirement header read from the first criterion. Measured: WBS-24.5's three criteria answer to THREE DIFFERENT requirements (AC-149 -> FR-155, AC-150 -> NFR-059, AC-151 -> NFR-060), so the generator still exits 2 on it, now with `FATAL: WBS-24.5: AC-150 answers to NFR-059 but AC-149 answers to FR-155; one header cannot describe both`. The multi-REQUIREMENT case and the multi-CRITERION case are different quantities, and DEF-116's own text conflates them by counting criteria; LL-015's rule that an instrument's output measures the thing the instrument counts and nothing else, applied to a guard rather than to a scanner. title: THE SLATE GENERATOR'S REGRESSION SUITE COUPLED ITS CASES TO LIVE LIFECYCLE STATUSES, SO PROMOTING ONE ROW DELETED A CALIBRATION'S SUBJECT WITHOUT DELETING THE CASE - AND IT FAILED LOUDLY ONLY BY LUCK. scripts/test-gen-slice-review-slate.py landed with #326 as the regression suite for DEF-117 and DEF-119. Each case copied the store to a scratch tree and set ONE row's lifecycle_status to Review, leaving every sibling as the live register happened to have it. That is a dependency on today's data in a suite whose whole purpose is to assert a PROPERTY of the generator. THE INSTANCE, hours later in the same session. WBS-25.1 was promoted to Implemented by DEC-092. The calibration case - which strips the DW-/DEC- citations out of a criterion-less item and asserts the generator STILL refuses it - mutated WBS-25.1 as before, but WBS-25.1 was no longer at Review, so the generator never looked at it. It rendered WBS-25.2 instead, an item that was never under test and that carries a DW-079 citation, exited 0, and the case failed. THE MUTATION STILL APPLIED AND THE GENERATOR STILL RAN; ONLY THE SUBJECT HAD GONE. ⚠⚠ THE LOUD FAILURE WAS LUCK, AND THAT IS THE WHOLE FINDING. The surviving Review row happened to carry a DW- citation, so the generator rendered it and exited 0 against an expected 2. Had that row instead lacked citations - which is one title-edit away, and is the normal state of an item early in its life - the generator would have exited 2 with the expected message for a COMPLETELY DIFFERENT REASON, and the calibration would have reported PASS while testing nothing. A calibration that can pass for the wrong reason is the hollow pass it exists to prevent, and it would have been silent from that moment on. THE FIX. Every case now STAGES THE WHOLE SLICE: the row under test is forced to Review, every sibling in that slice is forced out of Review, and the shape being tested is written into the title rather than inherited from it. The cases assert a property of the generator and are independent of which rows the register happens to hold at Review. Proof the coupling is gone: the calibration now passes with WBS-25.1 at Implemented, which is the exact live state that broke it. ⚠ THE GENERAL SHAPE, AND IT IS THIS PROJECT'S OWN: a test whose fixture is the live register is a test whose meaning changes when somebody does ordinary work. It is 'baselines are numbers, not properties' applied to a test fixture, and it was introduced by the same session that wrote the suite - so the suite guarding an instrument was itself the least-guarded thing in the change.
